stories.topic: From Rebel Without Restraints to Rebel With Rules
stories.summary: Amit opens and closes the episode with a self-portrait. At fifteen to seventeen he was 'a rebel without a cause', or, to alliterate, a rebel without restraints: he stayed up late, worked three days straight, drank beer with friends whenever he liked, skipped exercise and ate anything. Today he tries to be a rebel with rules: at least eight hours of sleep with enough REM and deep sleep, predictable meal times, a careful diet (especially after a recent health episode), and more exercise, though he admits that last one is still 'do as I say, don't do as I do.' He compares these rules to the countless algorithms that let an Elon Musk rocket be caught when it comes back.
stories.insight: This is the episode's thesis turned inward. A constitution constrains the state, not the people. In the same way, personal rules constrain your bad habits, not your freedom. They are the scaffolding from which bold, independent work can take off.
stories.quote: If you want to do bold imaginative things, if you want to be an independent thinker and independent doer, fight against convention, all of those are wonderful things and all of those require rules and rules set by you yourself.

stories.topic: Drunk With Happiness Over a 1977 Paper
stories.summary: While preparing for this episode, Ajay had an anxiety attack: had he forgotten something about Kydland and Prescott? So early that morning he reread the 1977 paper he first met in his first-year PhD coursework, when he was 'a happy, giddy child' studying macro and micro. He found he still knew all of it. But rereading it brought back the feeling of discovering these ideas for the first time. Amit had set up the moment by teasing that Ajay reads papers all night the way other people binge.
stories.insight: Foundational ideas reward rereading. Going back to a classic decades later can do more than refresh your memory. It can rekindle the original thrill of discovery, and that thrill is part of what keeps a lifetime of learning going.
stories.quote: I also just got a little drunk with happiness because just the whole memory, the feeling of being in first year PhD and discovering these things for the first time came back to me.

stories.summary: Ireland powered its growth with a very low corporate tax rate that drew global firms to build factories and offices there. Ajay would recommend low, ideally zero, corporate tax for India too. Now imagine a downturn or an earthquake, and a 'clever' policymaker who reasons that the factories are already built, so the firms are hostages, and raises the 5% rate for just two or three years. The move is popular, the press praises it, and it might even win an election. But firms plan on 5-, 10- and 25-year horizons, and turning an expected 8% dollar return on equity into 6% wrecks their calculations. Worse, once a firm has been socked, it assumes it can be socked again. So every future plan builds in a higher assumed tax rate or a higher risk premium, and the low-tax policy loses its pulling power for years.
stories.insight: Opportunism looks like a free win, but it destroys the credibility that made the original policy work. Economists treated this kind of clever exploitation as normal until the 1970s. The modern view is that a state that tries to be clever ends up weaker.
stories.quote: The state loses power by being opportunistic.

stories.topic: The Four-Bet That Stopped Meaning Aces
stories.summary: Most poker is exploitative: you spot a mistake the table keeps making, such as folding too much or bluffing too much, and adjust to profit from it. The trap is assuming the table won't adjust back. In the 2000s Amit read a canonical poker book which said that a four-bet (re-raising a re-raise) almost always means aces. By the time he was a professional, a four-bet was often nothing at all, because players were exploiting the people who had learned that rule. Ajay's quip: 'Everybody read the book and said, Oh, I can exploit this.'
stories.insight: People respond to your actions, so the world doesn't stand still while you exploit it. Amit applies the same logic to taxes. Assuming a higher tax rate brings in proportionally more revenue ignores how people adjust, and India's roughly 97% top tax rate in the 1970s did not produce a booming economy.
stories.quote: which is why exploitative poker is also automatically exploitable poker.

stories.topic: Julius Caesar and the Invention of Rule by Law
stories.summary: Ajay says Julius Caesar was no democrat: he destroyed the Roman Republic just as Rome was learning to disperse power. Ajay also counts him among the greatest human beings and thinkers who ever lived. Running a vast empire, Caesar did not want minions everywhere deciding for themselves how to use his coercive power, each one becoming a local tyrant. So he began writing laws and process manuals, so that everyone beneath him would act predictably under his authority. Caesar himself stayed unbound.
stories.insight: Even a strongman, purely to stay in control, sees that rules beat discretion for everyone below him. Amit points out that this is 'rule by law', which is quite different from 'rule of law', where the ruler too is subject to the law.
stories.quote: Julius Caesar destroyed the republic. I also happen to consider him one of the greatest human beings who ever lived.

stories.topic: The 1970s Oil Shock and Unhinged Expectations
stories.summary: When a central bank credibly promises stable inflation (India's RBI Act holds it to 4%), firms stop overreacting to one-off cost shocks and bond markets can price 25-year debt with confidence. During the 1970s oil shock, American policymakers were already watching people pay more for petrol and unemployment rise. They felt that raising rates would add to the misery of ordinary people, so they let inflation run 'for some time'. Firms and bond markets learned that inflation was no longer guaranteed, behaviour changed across the economy, and growth suffered.
stories.insight: Discretion in the name of compassion can unhinge expectations, and rebuilding them takes decades. That is why modern thinking says a central bank must hit its inflation target whatever is happening, whether an election, a crisis or a drought.
stories.quote: But the thing is, once you do this, you have unhinged the expectations of the economy.

stories.summary: Amit traces how India's 1991–2011 growth episode went bust. After the terror attacks in Bombay, the home minister had to be moved, and Manmohan Singh put his most capable man, P. Chidambaram, into the home ministry. Sonia Gandhi then gave finance to Pranab Mukherjee, whom Amit calls a 'wild evil courtier' with no knowledge of economics, and Manmohan Singh, who had health issues, did not take the portfolio himself. Mukherjee produced one disastrous measure after another. The worst was retrospective taxation: telling companies that new tax rules applied to the past too, so they owed back dues.
stories.insight: Trust is asymmetric: it takes decades to build and an instant to lose. Retrospective tax is the ultimate discretionary ambush, and it especially hurts foreign investors, whom India needs. Amit adds that good policy isn't a party matter. Between 1991 and 2011, different parties governed with the nation's interests at heart.
stories.quote: It strikes me that building trust can take decades, but losing trust can take an instant.

stories.summary: Amit draws on his episode with military historian Probal DasGupta. At Nathu La and Cho La, a local commander, General Sagat Singh, disobeyed an order from high command because he understood conditions on the ground, and this later helped India enormously. Yet an army only works if orders are followed. Amit's tentative answer is to build complexity into the rules so the rules themselves say when discretion applies. Ajay agrees: great militaries separate strategy, operations and tactics, and each level fully owns its own sphere.
stories.insight: Rules versus discretion is not an either/or choice. Good institutions decide which layer gets which discretion. Ajay's caveat for governments: what matters in the Kydland-Prescott sense is that the state's rules, however long, are known to the people.
stories.quote: In the army especially, where it is imperative to follow orders. You have to follow orders, otherwise a whole edifice can collapse. But at the same time you also need that local discretion.

stories.summary: Citing Clayton Christensen's innovator's dilemma, Amit notes that Kodak had the know-how to move into digital photography, but its rules, processes and incentives kept it stuck. Google, at least in the early 2000s, let employees spend part of their time on passion projects inside the company. Ajay agrees that firms need occasional big strategy pivots. Government, he says, is different: a city like Liverpool has wanted the same things for centuries, namely streets, parks, solid waste management, water and sanitation. The exception is war. The Russia-Ukraine war has set off an innovation spiral in drones and precision-guided munitions, and armies that keep fighting the last war get left behind.
stories.insight: Rules can fossilise firms, so smart firms design rules that leave room to disrupt themselves. Governments mostly deliver basics that don't change, and there predictability is the whole point.
stories.quote: You could also work on disrupting yourself. You would not have to go out and do that somewhere else. You could do it in Google itself, which I thought was very wise.

stories.summary: Many large Indian firms buying some humble part believe a hundred small suppliers are desperate to sell to them. So they drive brutal bargains, extract working-capital credit from small firms (which is backwards, since big firms have the cheaper capital), and practise gundagiri by opportunistically breaking the contract. The executives take pride in this machismo. But small firms build the treatment into their expectations and shade their bids upward. The bully ends up paying more than firms that behave well. Ajay would instead promise vendors swift payment and get better prices in return.
stories.insight: Dealing with vendors is a repeated game, and the price you get in an auction reflects your reputation. Opportunism that wins one procurement quietly loses you every future one.
stories.quote: So it's opportunistic and short term to think that in one procurement, in one situation, I will screw you over and I'll get an unusually good deal. But like what about the future?

stories.topic: The Parent Who Can't Bring Himself to Punish
stories.summary: A parent says, 'If you do X, I will punish you.' No parent actually wants to punish a child, so when the moment comes it is very tempting to let it go. But that is exactly how the parent loses credibility. A household run on mood, yes today and no tomorrow, leaves children confused, and they start working out how to game the parent instead of learning the guardrails.
stories.insight: Kydland and Prescott apply at home. Predictable, gradually evolving rules (not micromanagement) give children clearer boundaries than loving but erratic discretion.
stories.quote: And yet, when you do that, actually you've lost all your credibility, you've lost your commitment.

recommendations.item: Rules Rather than Discretion: The Inconsistency of Optimal Plans
recommendations.creator: Finn E. Kydland and Edward C. Prescott
recommendations.context: The 1977 Journal of Political Economy paper at the centre of the episode. Ajay first studied it in his PhD coursework and reread it the morning he prepared for this episode.
recommendations.reason: It is a landmark of the rational expectations revolution and, Ajay notes, part of the work behind both authors' Nobel Prizes. It made economists take credibility and commitment seriously and showed that a state which ties its own hands becomes more effective.

recommendations.creator: Rajnish Mehra and Edward Prescott
recommendations.context: Mentioned while introducing Prescott, via Ajay's friend Rajnish Mehra.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls it an 'amazing paper', co-written by a friend of the show with one of the authors of the episode's key paper.

recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's blog post, cited while discussing how to stop politicians from manipulating interest rates.
recommendations.reason: It sets out a concrete commitment device. The government-appointed governor is the channel for political pressure, so put the governor alongside four independent private economists, with five votes in total, so that only one vote is exposed to that pressure.

recommendations.item: The policy posture as an incomplete contract
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A blog post based on discussions with Josh Felman, cited when Amit asks how good policy can survive in India.
recommendations.reason: It explains why no law truly pre-commits the state, since any law can be amended tomorrow, and why policies last only when an intellectual community guards them.

recommendations.item: Why the RBI communication to government on the failure to meet inflation target must be placed in the public domain
recommendations.creator: The Indian Express
recommendations.context: Show-notes link tied to Ajay's point about central banks writing a public mea culpa letter when they miss the inflation target.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case for publishing the RBI's explanation for missing its target. A public mea culpa makes failure painful, and that pain is what makes the rule credible.

recommendations.creator: Gordon Tullock & James Buchanan
recommendations.context: Amit's end-of-episode recommendation.
recommendations.reason: Amit says it speaks directly to the episode's theme. He calls it a masterpiece: not an easy read, but a foundational book everyone who wants to understand the field should read.

recommendations.item: A rowing machine (the Concept2 is the most common)
recommendations.creator: Concept2
recommendations.context: Ajay's end-of-episode recommendation, after Amit made him show off his biceps on camera.
recommendations.reason: If you are lazy and will commit to only one exercise, make it rowing. It is cardio and works something like 80–85% of the body's muscles.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled while explaining why people instinctively want strongmen.
recommendations.reason: It explains how instincts shaped in small prehistoric tribes, such as zero-sum and top-down thinking, mislead us today, including our attraction to strong leaders.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced in Amit's poker analogy for opportunistic policy.
recommendations.reason: It covers in depth game-theory-optimal versus exploitative play and why exploitative play is itself exploitable.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's on-air recommendation after the monetary policy chapter.
recommendations.reason: It is the full story of inflation targeting, the canonical example of a rule, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s. It took more than fifteen years to become law, a lesson in how slowly good policy arrives.

recommendations.item: Don't Mess With the Exchange Rate (Episode 67)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited as an example of a real policy debate about which rule to adopt.
recommendations.reason: Choosing between an exchange-rate target and an inflation target is the kind of rule-level debate Ajay considers real public policy. He calls the exchange rate the most important price in the country.

recommendations.item: The Vintage Book of Indian Writing 1947–1997
recommendations.creator: Edited by Salman Rushdie & Elizabeth West
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Amit argues that communication is part of governance.
recommendations.reason: Its first chapter is 'Tryst with Destiny', which Ajay offers as evidence that great leaders combine thinking with the subtle ability to convey complex ideas.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Invoked when Amit asks how rules-not-discretion connects to ending India's poverty.
recommendations.reason: It makes the argument that growth is the only way out of poverty, which this episode connects to rules and credibility.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's starting point for asking how rules and local discretion coexist inside organisations.
recommendations.reason: It maps how Indian firms moved from regional satraps in the 1980s, to top-down 'imperial' firms with uniform best practices in the 1990s, to 'adaptive' firms that pair rules with local flexibility.

recommendations.item: Probal DasGupta Goes to the Himalayas With Books in His Bag (Episode 412 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The source of the General Sagat Singh story.
recommendations.reason: Amit discussed in detail with the military historian the tension between obeying orders and using local discretion.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Recalled in Ajay's international-relations example.
recommendations.reason: It explains why covert, opportunistic attacks, such as secretly crippling another country's payroll system, are the strategy of rogue nations and backfire in the long run.

recommendations.creator: Clayton Christensen
recommendations.context: Raised when Amit asks whether rules can become a straitjacket for firms.
recommendations.reason: It explains how dominant companies like Kodak can have the know-how to adapt yet fail, trapped by their own processes, priorities and incentives.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Referenced for Netflix as the 'honorable example' of a company that adapted.
recommendations.reason: It is the companion discussion on why big companies crumble when they can't adapt, and how some escape that fate.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's case study of a reform that unravelled.
recommendations.reason: It shows how a community of people with a shared philosophy built the NPS, and how the reversal followed once that community dispersed.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A second example of policy held together by an intellectual community.
recommendations.reason: It covers a 25-year stretch in which the Ministry of Finance, NSE, SEBI and academics worked together and got a lot done, and how things went wrong one by one after that group scattered.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay lays out three escalating arguments. First, public choice theory: the strongman is an ordinary person with wants, needs and flaws, so absolute power in his hands is a nightmare, and the answer is checks and balances, rule of law and dispersed power. Second, public administration: every strongman's minions become little tyrants, so even an autocrat wants rules to bind them. Third, the economists' contribution: the state itself becomes more effective when it gives up discretion. That third point clashes with the macho instinct of most civil servants, who enjoy granting favours to supplicants.
core_ideas.quote: the state becomes more effective, not less, when it shackles its own hands with rules and takes away discretion.

core_ideas.explanation: Our attraction to strongmen is hardwired from prehistoric tribes of about 150 people, where top-down, zero-sum thinking worked, and we have to consciously fight it. 'Weak' here doesn't mean weak in character or intellect. It means a leader whose ability to act on whims is boxed in by laws and institutions. Amit cites James Buchanan's design test: build a system so robust that even if the worst person imaginable, whether Hitler or anyone, rises to the top, they can't do much damage.
core_ideas.quote: you should design a system which is so strong with such checks and balances built in that if the worst person you can imagine is in charge, they can't do much damage.

core_ideas.concept: Rule by Law vs Rule of Law
core_ideas.explanation: Under rule by law, the ruler writes laws that everyone else must obey but stays above them himself, which is the Caesar model. Under rule of law, the ruler is also subject to the law and cannot override it. The first makes a strongman more efficient. Only the second actually restrains him.
core_ideas.quote: Julius Caesar is not enveloped in law. Julius Caesar has no checks and balances. He has arbitrary power, but he wants everybody else to operate in a predictable rules based way.

core_ideas.concept: You Are Not Wood, You Are Not Stones: Rational Expectations
core_ideas.explanation: Until the 1960s, economists modelled a smart, optimising state ruling over passive, credulous people. The rational expectations revolution of the late 60s and 70s assumed instead that people look ahead, watch the policymaker and adjust. Ajay disowns the word 'rational', because people aren't perfect Bayesian computers. The real point is that they aren't fools either. So any surprise the state springs changes how people behave afterwards, through things like higher risk premia and padded tax assumptions.
core_ideas.quote: You are not wood, you are not stones, but men. And being men, you will optimize.

core_ideas.concept: Anchored Inflation as a Public Good
core_ideas.explanation: Once everyone believes inflation will be 4%, firms stop panicking over one-off cost shocks and price strategically. Bond markets can also price 25-year debt, because long-term interest rates are essentially a bet on inflation. India's RBI Act holds the RBI accountable for 4%. But with a short track record and middling performance, Ajay says it will take decades to anchor the minds of firms, savers and pension planners.
core_ideas.quote: That the highest contribution that the Indian central bank can make to growth in India is to stabilize everybody's mind.

core_ideas.concept: Policymaking Is Rule Design, Not Day-to-Day Decisions
core_ideas.explanation: The primitive model of governance is a person who looks at each situation and decides. In a rules-based world, the real intellectual work is designing the rule ('if state X arises, we do Y'). After that, officials simply carry out a publicly stated manual. A good country puts its best and brightest into imagining incentive-compatible rules, as with the Constituent Assembly, the NPS and inflation targeting.
core_ideas.quote: So the work of doing public policy is actually more meta. It is about imagining one rule at a time.

core_ideas.concept: Credibility and Commitment Are the State's Real Power
core_ideas.explanation: A government that flips back and forth, with a tariff one day and none the next, gets discounted by everyone, and private uncertainty rises. Power comes from announcing something and then doing it, again and again, with no gap between words and deeds. Populist regimes believe their propaganda can float free of their actions, which is why people say 'watch not what they say, but watch what they do'. That decoupling doesn't last, because people are smart.
core_ideas.quote: So in the world of inflation targeting, there's a beautiful slogan. We say that say what you will do and then do what you just said.

core_ideas.explanation: This is the opposite of strongman logic: you gain power by deliberately giving it up. The state lacks credibility, so it builds mechanisms that make breaking its own rules costly. Ajay's examples: a monetary policy committee where four independent economists outvote the politically exposed governor; New Zealand-style bonuses for central bankers who hit the target and money lost when they miss, all announced by press release; and a public mea culpa letter that diagnoses what went wrong (data, models, analysis or transmission). These devices work because leaders care most about the respect of their peers.
core_ideas.quote: It is wise and efficient for the state to shed discretion, to shed power, to lose power, to create a series of provisions and mechanisms through which violating the rule will become unpleasant for the state.

core_ideas.concept: Communication Is Part of Governance, Not Advertising
core_ideas.explanation: We usually treat government communication as propaganda wrapped around the real work. Amit argues that consistent communication matched by action is itself governance, because it builds the trust that drives economic behaviour. Where rules can't spell everything out, leaders must explain their philosophy and their view of the world in speeches, so people can predict how they'll act in situations nobody foresaw. Ajay notes that such speeches have nearly died out in India. Done badly, the process runs backwards: a slogan comes first and drives the policy.
core_ideas.quote: Communication is central. It is so important, therefore of a part of governance itself. It is not advertising, it is part of the product.

core_ideas.concept: Rules Can Be Complex, Just Not Surprising
core_ideas.explanation: Rules-based doesn't mean simplistic; Ajay says a rule needn't be 160 bytes and can run to 16,000 pages. You could issue a government bond that, by its own terms, pays zero interest in any year real GDP growth is negative. That is fine because it was promised upfront. What is not fine is skipping interest payments after the fact because 'we had a bad year'. The test is whether the rule was known in advance, not how long it is: a world of rules, not deals.
core_ideas.quote: You're allowed to go complexity, but you're not allowed to expropriate people.

core_ideas.concept: India Needs Rules More, Not Less
core_ideas.explanation: It's tempting to treat Kydland-Prescott as a luxury for rich countries. Ajay argues the reverse. If German firms and bondholders are skeptical of the Bundesbank, Indians, after a long history of bad state behaviour, are ten times more so. So Indian policymakers need tighter handcuffs, louder communication, and daily press conferences and unscripted town halls where they face hard questions.
core_ideas.quote: So Kydland and Prescott and rules and discretion should not be seen as something that is done in advanced economies. You need it even more in India, given the institutional mistrust.

core_ideas.concept: Rules Are the Machinery of Growth
core_ideas.explanation: Growth comes from high-productivity firms controlling large amounts of labour and capital. Such firms are built over decades by people who commit their money, passion, time and even their children to them. Whether anyone makes that bet depends on the state. Every expropriation, every sudden rule change, every monopoly PSU or rigged game favouring a national champion teaches investors, Indian and foreign, to hold back, diversify abroad and wait and see. The result is low GDP growth.
core_ideas.quote: All these fears add up to a wet blanket.

core_ideas.concept: Layering Discretion: Strategy, Operations, Tactics and Subsidiarity
core_ideas.explanation: Rules and discretion can be divided between levels. Militaries give strategy to the top, operations to the middle and tactics to the field. Amit adapts the subsidiarity principle: decide the 'why' at the top, the 'what' a level below, and the 'how' locally, where the best information is. Ajay grounds it in India's diversity. Local priorities and costs differ: a teacher costs something different in Bihar than in Kerala, and a malarial city faces problems a desert town doesn't. So monetary policy belongs with the Union, a few things with the states, and most things with cities.
core_ideas.quote: So in fact, this desire for predictability and rules and yet handling the heterogeneity of the world is the logic of decentralization.

core_ideas.concept: Policy Is an Incomplete Contract: Communities Pour the Concrete
core_ideas.explanation: No law truly pre-commits the state. Inflation targeting is an ordinary act of parliament that could be amended tomorrow. Ajay mocks the caricature of economists whispering into the ear of a ruler like Aurangzeb, because the next whisperer can undo it. What actually makes policy last is a broad intellectual community of owners and guardians who watch the space, write and criticise. The NPS and Indian financial reform both thrived while their communities existed and unravelled once those communities dispersed. The bipartisan US foreign-policy consensus held for the same reason.
core_ideas.quote: Things only stay in place when they're surrounded, when they're ensconced in that community that will watch.

core_ideas.concept: Opportunism Is Never Free: Contracts, Sentencing, Treaties
core_ideas.explanation: The same logic applies far beyond economics. Between firms, renegotiating a contract opportunistically just leads counterparties to price in the risk. In criminal law, broad judicial discretion over sentences opens a Pandora's box of doubts about fair play and invites criminals to bet on leniency, so Ajay favours sentencing guidelines. In international relations, where no court can enforce anything, a strongman who walks out of a treaty gets cheered at home, but every other treaty partner learns not to trust his country. In each case the short-term win is paid for over the long run.
core_ideas.quote: You're better off not being opportunistic. You're better off not being exploitative. You're better off playing by rules of the game.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's one-line summary of the personal version of rules over discretion. Steady routines in sleep, food and exercise free up energy and attention for bold, creative thinking. Discipline is what makes the rebellion effective.
core_ideas.quote: Be quiet and predictable in your life, so that you can be explosive and creative in your ideas.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's self-diagnosis riffing on 'Rebel Without a Cause': as a teenager he was a rebel without a cause, 'or if we wish to alliterate, a rebel without restraints', and today he is 'a rebel with rules.'
A sly dig at dynasties: 'we instinctively prefer strong men, or even strong women sometimes, especially if they're from a family of an earlier strong man.'
Ajay describing the policymaker who wants to squeeze trapped foreign firms: 'the clever policy maker, okay, it's Indian IAS level of IQ.'
Amit to listeners: 'Ajay Shah reads papers the way other adolescent boys watch porn.' You start one paper at 9 PM and suddenly it's 4 AM and you've gone through forty.

Ajay's caricature of how many economists think policy happens: they 'whisper in the ears of Aurangzeb and miraculously some policy will happen', until Aurangzeb 'wakes up from the wrong side of the bed' or someone else whispers in his ear.
Ajay offers the aphorism 'Be quiet and predictable in your life, so that you can be explosive and creative in your ideas', and Amit deadpans: 'Have you ever considered Twitter?'

Amit makes Ajay roll up his sleeve and flex for the camera ('Nomsita, can we zoom, please?'), then points out that the biceps came from a rules-based regime, not from doing whatever exercise he felt like.

Ajay pitches rowing to anyone who is 'a lazy bum' or 'a sleepy Bengali'. Amit hits back with a Hindi pun: his Bengali melodrama makes him want to weep copiously and become a 'rona' (crying) machine. He adds that Bengal gave India Rabindra Sangeet and Satyajit Ray, while Gujarat gave 'a diet that is guaranteed to produce diabetes. Well done.'

Amit on the final recommendations: 'I am recommending a geeky scholarly book and he is recommending a rowing machine… This is a man of action. So I guess the second half of your life will be more action than thought.'

Mark Antony's speech over Caesar's corpse in Shakespeare's Julius Caesar ('You are not wood, you are not stones, but men'), which Ajay adapts into his personal economics slogan: '…and being men, you will optimize.'

Ram Rajya and the mai-baap state: Ajay says we grow up imagining the strongman will be a Ram, a ruler who grants wishes 'straight out of Hindu mythology', and that a good country is one where he can grant very few.
Indira Gandhi's 1970s top income tax rate of about 97% (Amit's figure), offered as proof that pushing rates up doesn't bring in proportionally more and didn't make India a booming economy.
'Tryst with Destiny' as the first chapter of Salman Rushdie's anthology of Indian writing, used as evidence that great leaders pair thought with eloquent articulation.

From an earlier decentralisation discussion: Japan has about thirty varieties of Kit Kat, while India has 'only one Maggi, one Kit Kat'. Amit uses it to show how uniform rules can ignore local tastes.
Ajay's pitch for a future episode, 'Legitimacy: Why and How', on legitimacy as the subtle state in which 'the people are in harmony with the project of the state.'
